newsitem.title: UK: Buba caps dollar but rally not over yet - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Buba caps dollar but rally not over yet - analysts.

text.p: The dollar romped to 34-month highs against the mark in early Europe, only to skid downhill when the Bundesbank insisted it did not believe the currency should climb further.

A report from news agency MNSI that Germany would welcome further dollar strength boosted the U.S. unit overnight, but the bank said it continued to support the view, recently expressed by the Group of Seven, that the dollar had already corrected.
Analysts said the Bundesbank had probably capped the dollar for today but believed the rally still had further to run.
"I think we've seen the highs for the day, but I doubt we've even seen the highs for the week," said Peter von Maydell, senior currency economist at UBS in London.
The dollar was quoted at 1.6790/95 marks at 1109 GMT, off a session low of 1.6745 but a far cry from the 1.6935 peak it scaled in early trade, its best level since April 1994.
Dollar/yen slipped to 123.54/59 from its high of 124.48. Both pairs stuck above late Tuesday's European levels of 1.6715/25 and 122.75/85, however.
Analysts said the response to the Bundesbank statement was symptomatic of a market on tenterhooks for intervention.
"Whenever you see a big move there's going to be sensitivity but it's just a case of wait and see," said Brian Hilliard, chief economist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull here.

Analysts said concerted intervention at current levels was unlikely -- but did not rule out unilateral Japanese action. "Very near-term it could be that the Japanese finally lose patience and decide to do somthing themselves," said Nigel Richardson, international economist at Yamaichi.
Japan's Ministry of Finance fuelled such fears this morning saying Japan would "take appropriate measures to tackle any excessive moves" in the forex markets.
Analysts said levels around 125 yen would really set market tongues wagging about Japanese intervention. Germany and the U.S. had little interest in selling dollars, they said.

U.S. January retail sales and producer price data due out tomorrow and Friday should exacerbate the woes of the yen and, in particular, the mark as they highlight the health of the U.S. economy compared to those of its G3 fellows, analysts said.

"The (German) labour market, the increasingly tight fiscal policy and the very loose monetary policy with bund yields hitting post-war lows yesterday are all profoundly negative for the deutschemark," said UBS' Von Maydell.
Today's second leg of the U.S. Treasury quarterly refunding -- the sale of $12 billion of 10-year notes -- is likely to go well and should support the dollar, analysts said.
The market absorbed yesterday's $17.75 billion of three-year notes with relative ease. Thirty-year bonds go on sale Thursday.
In its official statement, the Bundesbank said it still backed the view that currency misalignments had been corrected, as stated by the G7 after last weekend's meeting in Berlin.
"The statement said the dollar has been corrected, and it was made at a rate of 1.65 marks," said chief Bundesbank spokesman Manfred Koerber.
MNSI had quoted German officials as saying they would welcome a dollar rise to a range of 1.70 to 1.75 marks.
Elsewhere, the U.S. currency zoomed to a 34-month high of 1.4500 Swiss francs in early Europe but had retreated to 1.4414/24 by 1146 GMT, versus late Tuesday's rate of 1.4330/50.

Sterling/mark profited from the dollar's strength, powering to a new 52-month high of 2.7685 marks before easing back to 2.7520/30 by 1148 GMT. It drew strength from a 67,800 fall in UK January unemployment -- over twice the forecast drop -- and a renewed call for monetary tightening in the Bank of England's quarterly inflation report. -- London Newsroom +44-171542-8968
